# Constrained decoding {#sec-constrained-decoding} **You will learn:** - what a grammar does to the model's next-token probabilities, and why it can only repair syntax; - how a grammar for the DSL and one for Python are written and checked against every gold program; - how much of the gap between the untuned and the fine-tuned model a grammar can close. A model that writes a program can write one that does not run: a stray word, a missing parenthesis, a code fence. Chapters @sec-dsl and @sec-tokens stopped short of fixing this. A **grammar** does: at every step, it lists the tokens that can continue a valid program, and the decoder gives every other token probability zero. The model still chooses, among the tokens that are allowed. This chapter runs the grammar on the untuned and the fine-tuned model, with the DSL and with Python. ## The grammars The DSL grammar is that of @sec-dsl in the EBNF of the `xgrammar` library. The Python grammar describes the forms that `to_python` writes (@sec-python-format): assignments to `v`, then `ans = …`, with numbers, names, the operators `+ - * / ** >` and parentheses. It is narrower than the safe evaluator, so a model that follows it cannot leave the evaluator's subset. Each has a **[bounded](901_glossary.qmd#gloss-bounded-grammar)** variant that limits a number to the digits the gold programs use: a grammar guarantees syntax and not termination, and with an unbounded number rule a model can keep writing digits up to the generation limit. ::: {#e8d008b3 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from convfinqa import grammars print(grammars.python_grammar().strip()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` root ::= (assignment "\n")* final assignment ::= "v" [0-9]+ " = " comparison final ::= "ans = " comparison comparison ::= sum (" > " sum)? sum ::= product ((" + " | " - ") product)* product ::= power ((" * " | " / ") power)* power ::= atom (" ** " atom)? atom ::= number | "-" number | "v" [0-9]+ | "(" comparison ")" | "(-" number ")" number ::= [0-9]+ ("." [0-9]+)? | "." [0-9]+ ``` ::: ::: ::: {#b5016b06 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd from transformers import AutoTokenizer from convfinqa.artifacts import artifact, get from convfinqa.constrained import compile_grammar, grammar_accepts from convfinqa.dsl import python_format tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507") dsl = compile_grammar(tok, grammars.dsl_grammar(), vocab_size=151936) py = compile_grammar(tok, grammars.python_grammar(), vocab_size=151936) CASES = { "subtract(5, 3), divide(#0, 3)": dsl, "subtract(5, 3), divide(#0, 3) because": dsl, "```add(1, 2)```": dsl, "ans = (5 - 3) / 3": py, "v0 = 5 - 3\nans = v0 / 3": py, "ans = round(2.567, 1)": py, "```python\nans = 1 + 2\n```": py, "The answer is ans = 2": py, } pd.DataFrame([ { "text": text.replace("\n", "; "), "grammar": "DSL" if g is dsl else "Python", "accepted": grammar_accepts(g, text), } for text, g in CASES.items() ]).set_index("text") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## One decoding step The mask is a list of the tokens that may come next. To see it, we feed a prefix to the grammar and ask which of the model's 151\,936 output tokens remain possible. ::: {#522c2d77 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import torch import xgrammar as xgr VOCAB = 151936 def allowed_tokens(compiled, prefix: str) -> list[int]: """The ids of the tokens that may follow `prefix` under the grammar.""" matcher = xgr.GrammarMatcher(compiled, terminate_without_stop_token=True) assert prefix == "" or matcher.accept_string(prefix) mask = xgr.allocate_token_bitmask(1, VOCAB) matcher.fill_next_token_bitmask(mask) logits = torch.zeros(1, VOCAB) xgr.apply_token_bitmask_inplace(logits, mask) return torch.nonzero(torch.isfinite(logits[0])).flatten().tolist() STEPS = { "start of the answer": "", "after `subtract(`": "subtract(", "after `subtract(5, 3), `": "subtract(5, 3), ", } step_ids = {name: allowed_tokens(dsl, prefix) for name, prefix in STEPS.items()} pd.DataFrame([ { "position": name, "tokens allowed": len(ids), "a few of them": " ".join(repr(tok.decode([i])) for i in ids[:12]), } for name, ids in step_ids.items() ]).set_index("position") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: {#cd96afd7 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} #HEAVY # the first token of the untuned model's answer to the first turn of the # first conversation, without examples and without a grammar first = next(get("untuned_val_e0p_0_pred").jsonl("predictions.jsonl")) first_token = tok.encode(first["output"], add_special_tokens=False)[0] assert first_token not in step_ids["start of the answer"] assert len(step_ids["start of the answer"]) < 100 ``` ::: At the start of an answer, 39 tokens are allowed: digits, a minus sign, a point, and the first letters of the operators and of `const_`. The untuned model's own first token for the first turn, without examples, is '\`\`\`', the start of a code fence. It is not among them. ::: {.callout-note title="Under the hood: what the processor does to the logits"} The model produces one score (logit) per token. Before the next token is chosen, the processor sets the score of every token that the grammar does not allow to minus infinity. After the softmax those tokens have probability zero and the others share the whole probability between them, in the proportions the model gave them. Greedy decoding then picks the allowed token with the highest score. The model's preferences among valid continuations are untouched, and this is why a grammar can only repair syntax: it never makes the model prefer the correct operation. The matcher keeps the parse state, so the mask is recomputed after every token. `xgrammar` prechecks the tokens whose validity does not depend on the parse stack and checks only the others at run time [@dong2024xgrammar]. ::: ## The code A run with a grammar is the run without one, with the logits processor added: the same prompts, the same greedy decoding, one prompt at a time. `convfinqa.constrained_eval` holds the generator. The name of a run says which bound the number rule has (`free` or `bounded`). The runs without a grammar are the ones of @sec-baseline, @sec-python-format and @sec-training, and are not repeated. ::: {#b4672b30 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} @artifact( "constrained_untuned_{split}_{variant}_{seed}_{mode}_{bounds}", deps=["train_val_split", "eval_turns", "example_sets"], files=["configs/baseline.json"], heavy=True, ) def build_constrained_untuned( out, deps, files, *, split: str, variant: str, seed: int, mode: str, bounds: str ): """Generate the untuned model's DSL answer for every turn, under the DSL grammar. ## The same prompt, with the grammar off and on {#sec-constrained-results} Validation turns only (@sec-formatting), predicted history, greedy, one attempt, an invalid answer counts as wrong. Each row is one prompt run twice, with the same decoding and the grammar on or off, on the same turns, so the difference is paired. The grammar is the unbounded one (`free`); @sec-constrained-bounds compares it with the bounded one. ::: {#9b2b9393 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} #HEAVY import re from convfinqa.stats import bootstrap_accuracy, paired_difference SYSTEMS = { "untuned DSL": ( get("scores_untuned_val_e3p_0_pred"), get("scores_constrained_untuned_val_e3p_0_pred_free"), ), "untuned Python": ( get("scores_python_untuned_val_e3_0_pred"), get("scores_constrained_python_untuned_val_e3_0_pred_free"), ), "fine-tuned DSL": ( get("scores_tuned_val_main_0_pred"), get("scores_constrained_tuned_val_main_0_pred_free"), ), } off = {k: list(v[0].jsonl("scores.jsonl")) for k, v in SYSTEMS.items()} on = {k: list(v[1].jsonl("scores.jsonl")) for k, v in SYSTEMS.items()} off_sum = {k: v[0].json("summary.json") for k, v in SYSTEMS.items()} on_sum = {k: v[1].json("summary.json") for k, v in SYSTEMS.items()} off_ci = {k: bootstrap_accuracy(v) for k, v in off.items()} on_ci = {k: bootstrap_accuracy(v) for k, v in on.items()} gain = {k: paired_difference(on[k], off[k]) for k in SYSTEMS} n_val = off_sum["untuned DSL"]["n"] assert all(s["n"] == n_val for s in [*off_sum.values(), *on_sum.values()]) pct = lambda x: f"{100 * x:.1f}%" pts = lambda x: f"{100 * x:+.1f}" rows = [] for k in SYSTEMS: for label, ci, summary in [ ("off", off_ci, off_sum), ("on", on_ci, on_sum) ]: rows.append({ "system": k, "grammar": label, "accuracy": pct(ci[k]["accuracy"]), "95% interval": f"[{pct(ci[k]['low'])}, {pct(ci[k]['high'])}]", "invalid": pct(summary[k]["invalid_rate"]), "hit the limit": pct(summary[k]["truncated"] / n_val), }) pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index(["system", "grammar"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}

Accuracy rises by \+3\.3 points for the DSL and \+3\.8 for Python, and both paired intervals exclude zero. That is less than half of the invalid output that disappeared, so most of the turns the grammar rescues are valid programs that are still wrong. The fine-tuned model has almost no invalid answers to start with (0\.1% without the grammar, 0\.1% with it), and the grammar moves its accuracy by \+0\.1 points. ### Number turns and program turns A *number turn* is one whose gold program is a single number from the page; a *program turn* has operations (@sec-convfinqa). ::: {#26a76bdc .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} #HEAVY KINDS = ["number", "program"] by_kind = { (k, state): summary[k]["by_number_turn"] for k in SYSTEMS for state, summary in [("off", off_sum), ("on", on_sum)] } pd.DataFrame([ { "system": k, "kind of turn": kind, "turns": by_kind[(k, "off")][kind]["n"], "grammar off": pct(by_kind[(k, "off")][kind]["accuracy"]), "grammar on": pct(by_kind[(k, "on")][kind]["accuracy"]), } for k in SYSTEMS for kind in KINDS ]).set_index(["system", "kind of turn"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}

A number turn is a single number and has almost no syntax to get wrong; a program has brackets, commas and references to earlier steps. ## What the grammar cannot fix {#sec-constrained-gap} How far does an untuned model with the best prompt and a grammar get towards the fine-tuned one? The grammar only repairs syntax, so there is a ceiling: an untuned model whose every invalid answer became a correct one would score its accuracy plus its invalid rate. ::: {#2d0c2aef .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} #HEAVY tuned_off = off_ci["fine-tuned DSL"]["accuracy"] tuned_on = on_ci["fine-tuned DSL"]["accuracy"] gap = {} for k in ["untuned DSL", "untuned Python"]: start = off_ci[k]["accuracy"] gap[k] = { "ceiling": start + off_sum[k]["invalid_rate"], "with grammar": on_ci[k]["accuracy"], "total gap": tuned_off - start, "closed": (on_ci[k]["accuracy"] - start) / (tuned_off - start), } assert gap[k]["ceiling"] < tuned_off, k vs_tuned = paired_difference( on["fine-tuned DSL"], on["untuned DSL"] ) assert vs_tuned["low"] > 0 pd.DataFrame([ { "system": k, "no grammar": pct(off_ci[k]["accuracy"]), "ceiling": pct(g["ceiling"]), "with grammar": pct(g["with grammar"]), "fine-tuned, no grammar": pct(tuned_off), "share of the gap closed": pct(g["closed"]), } for k, g in gap.items() ]).set_index("system") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: For the DSL, the ceiling is 73\.5%, below the fine-tuned model's 83\.5%; for Python it is 73\.4%. Even a grammar that made every invalid answer correct could not reach the fine-tuned model. The grammar closes 12\.5% of the gap for the DSL and 20\.2% for Python (the Python gap is measured against the same fine-tuned DSL model). With the grammar on both, the fine-tuned DSL model is \+23\.1 points ahead of the untuned one (interval [\+19\.6, \+26\.7]). What is left is choosing the operations and the numbers. In the error kinds of @sec-baseline, the untuned DSL with the grammar still has 260 turns with different operations from the gold program, 79 with the same operations and different numbers, and 91 with the same shape and a different answer. The fine-tuned model has 59, 76 and 49. The classifier compares the operations first, so a turn with the wrong operations and the wrong numbers is counted once, as wrong operations. What fine-tuning changes most is the first of these. ## Description or enforcement? {#sec-constrained-2x2} The plain system message names no syntax rules for the DSL; the description message spells them out. They are two ways to tell the model the syntax, and the grammar is a third. The 2×2 below, with three examples, separates them. ::: {#bf63e5f7 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} #HEAVY CELLS = { ("plain", "off"): get("scores_untuned_val_e3p_0_pred"), ("plain", "on"): get("scores_constrained_untuned_val_e3p_0_pred_free"), ("description", "off"): get("scores_untuned_val_e3d_0_pred"), ("description", "on"): get("scores_constrained_untuned_val_e3d_0_pred_free"), } cell = {k: list(h.jsonl("scores.jsonl")) for k, h in CELLS.items()} cell_sum = {k: h.json("summary.json") for k, h in CELLS.items()} cell_ci = {k: bootstrap_accuracy(v) for k, v in cell.items()} enforce = { p: paired_difference(cell[(p, "on")], cell[(p, "off")]) for p in ["plain", "description"] } describe = { g: paired_difference(cell[("description", g)], cell[("plain", g)]) for g in ["off", "on"] } for p in enforce: assert enforce[p]["low"] > 0, p # the two intervals for the grammar's gain overlap assert ( enforce["plain"]["low"] < enforce["description"]["high"] and enforce["description"]["low"] < enforce["plain"]["high"] ) # with the grammar on, the description is the lower of the two prompts assert describe["on"]["high"] < 0 assert ( cell_sum[("description", "on")]["by_kind"]["bad_reference"] > cell_sum[("plain", "on")]["by_kind"]["bad_reference"] ) pd.DataFrame([ { "system message": p, "grammar": g, "accuracy": pct(cell_ci[(p, g)]["accuracy"]), "invalid": pct(cell_sum[(p, g)]["invalid_rate"]), } for (p, g) in CELLS ]).set_index(["system message", "grammar"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: The grammar helps with either message: \+3\.3 points with the plain one (interval [\+1\.9, \+4\.9]) and \+2\.0 with the description ([\+0\.9, \+3\.2]). The two intervals overlap, so this run does not show that the gain differs. Changing the plain message for the description changes accuracy by \-1\.9 points without a grammar ([\-3\.9, \+0\.1]) and by \-3\.2 with one ([\-5\.4, \-1\.1]). With the description the grammar brings the invalid rate from 17\.1% to 5\.3%, against 16\.4% to 1\.3% with the plain message. What remains with the description is mostly references to steps that do not exist (`bad_reference`: 58 turns, against 10 with the plain message), which no grammar of this kind rules out. So the description does not make the grammar redundant, and the grammar does not make the description worth having: with the grammar on, the description is the lower of the two. ## Without examples {#sec-constrained-e0} The three-example prompts show the format twice over: in the examples, and in the model's own earlier answers when they are valid. The prompt with no examples (`e0p`, the training prompt) shows it in neither. Without a grammar, the model with its own history is at the floor (@sec-python-untuned). ::: {#5ae329e0 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} #HEAVY E0 = { "grammar off, predicted history": get("scores_untuned_val_e0p_0_pred"), "grammar on, predicted history": get( "scores_constrained_untuned_val_e0p_0_pred_free" ), "grammar off, gold history": get("scores_untuned_val_e0p_0_gold"), } e0 = {k: list(h.jsonl("scores.jsonl")) for k, h in E0.items()} e0_sum = {k: h.json("summary.json") for k, h in E0.items()} first_turn = lambda rows: [r for r in rows if r["turn"] == 0] follow_up = lambda rows: [r for r in rows if r["turn"] > 0] acc = lambda rows: sum(r["correct"] for r in rows) / len(rows) e0_gain = paired_difference( e0["grammar on, predicted history"], e0["grammar off, predicted history"] ) off_first = acc(first_turn(e0["grammar off, predicted history"])) on_first = acc(first_turn(e0["grammar on, predicted history"])) on_follow = acc(follow_up(e0["grammar on, predicted history"])) gold_follow = acc(follow_up(e0["grammar off, gold history"])) assert e0_gain["low"] > 0.1 assert on_first > 10 * off_first assert on_follow < gold_follow pd.DataFrame([ { "run": k, "all turns": pct(acc(rows)), "first turns": pct(acc(first_turn(rows))), "follow-ups": pct(acc(follow_up(rows))), "invalid": pct(e0_sum[k]["invalid_rate"]), "hit the limit": pct(e0_sum[k]["truncated"] / n_val), } for k, rows in e0.items() ]).set_index("run") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ```{=html}

The first turn has no history, so its change is the effect of the grammar alone: from 0\.7% to 16\.3%. The grammar is the only thing here that tells the model what an answer looks like, and it is enough for some answers. The follow-up turns reach 22\.5% with the grammar and the model's own history. With the gold history and no grammar they reach 38\.3%. The two runs differ in the history (valid but mostly wrong, against correct) and in the grammar, so this does not separate what each contributes. Many of these answers do not stop: 27\.9% of the turns hit the generation limit, with digits that keep coming. That is what the bounded grammar is for. ## Bounding the numbers {#sec-constrained-bounds} A grammar guarantees syntax, not termination. The bounded variant allows at most the digits that the gold programs use (ten before the point, four after it), so a run of digits must end. ::: {#ffeef097 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} #HEAVY BOUNDS = { "untuned DSL, three examples": ( get("scores_constrained_untuned_val_e3p_0_pred_free"), get("scores_constrained_untuned_val_e3p_0_pred_bounded"), ), "untuned DSL, no examples": ( get("scores_constrained_untuned_val_e0p_0_pred_free"), get("scores_constrained_untuned_val_e0p_0_pred_bounded"), ), } free = {k: list(v[0].jsonl("scores.jsonl")) for k, v in BOUNDS.items()} bounded = {k: list(v[1].jsonl("scores.jsonl")) for k, v in BOUNDS.items()} free_sum = {k: v[0].json("summary.json") for k, v in BOUNDS.items()} bounded_sum = {k: v[1].json("summary.json") for k, v in BOUNDS.items()} bound_gain = {k: paired_difference(bounded[k], free[k]) for k in BOUNDS} for k in BOUNDS: assert not bound_gain[k]["excludes_zero"], k assert ( bounded_sum[k]["truncated"] < free_sum[k]["truncated"] ), k assert bounded_sum["untuned DSL, no examples"]["truncated"] == 0 pd.DataFrame([ { "run": k, "free": pct(free_sum[k]["accuracy"]), "bounded": pct(bounded_sum[k]["accuracy"]), "bounded − free (points)": pts(bound_gain[k]["difference"]), "95% paired interval": f"[{pts(bound_gain[k]['low'])}, {pts(bound_gain[k]['high'])}]", "hit the limit, free": free_sum[k]["truncated"], "hit the limit, bounded": bounded_sum[k]["truncated"], } for k in BOUNDS ]).set_index("run") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ```{=html}

So the unbounded grammar was not hiding accuracy, and the numbers in the rest of the chapter are those of the unbounded one. The bounded grammar is the safer one to use when a run must end, and costs nothing here. ## The time it takes {#sec-constrained-time} ::: {#3cee4a93 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} #HEAVY def log_seconds(handle): text = (handle.path / "build.log").read_text() return int(re.findall(r"done: \d+ turns in (\d+) s", text)[-1]) def tokens(handle): return sum(r["new_tokens"] for r in handle.jsonl("predictions.jsonl")) RUNS = { "untuned DSL": ( get("untuned_val_e3p_0_pred"), get("constrained_untuned_val_e3p_0_pred_free"), ), "untuned Python": ( get("python_untuned_val_e3_0_pred"), get("constrained_python_untuned_val_e3_0_pred_free"), ), "fine-tuned DSL": ( get("tuned_val_main_0_pred"), get("constrained_tuned_val_main_0_pred_free"), ), } timing = { k: { "off": (log_seconds(a), tokens(a)), "on": (log_seconds(b), tokens(b)), } for k, (a, b) in RUNS.items() } assert all(t["on"][0] <= t["off"][0] for t in timing.values()) assert all(t["on"][1] <= t["off"][1] for t in timing.values()) pd.DataFrame([ { "system": k, "seconds, off": t["off"][0], "seconds, on": t["on"][0], "tokens generated, off": f"{t['off'][1]:,}", "tokens generated, on": f"{t['on'][1]:,}", } for k, t in timing.items() ]).set_index("system") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ```{=html}

The runs were made in separate sessions, and the runs without a grammar generated at least as many tokens (invalid answers can run on). What the table can say is that no run with the grammar took longer than the run without it (the largest ratio is 0\.91). The overhead of the grammar is not measured in this book. ## Discussion {#sec-constrained-discussion} A grammar fixes the form and leaves the content, and the results above are what that looks like. Two pieces of related work are worth comparing. - **Format restrictions can hurt reasoning.** @tam2024speak compare language models restricted to structured output formats such as JSON or XML with free-form answers. They report a drop in reasoning ability under the restriction, larger for stricter formats. That concerns a model that reasons in the text it writes and is then made to write it in a format. Here the output is the program: there is no free text for the grammar to cut short, and the fine-tuned model does not change under the grammar. This chapter's runs do not test their claim. - **FinQA's decoder was restricted too.** The program generator of the original FinQA model takes its output tokens from three sources: the tokens of the question and the retrieved facts (the numbers), the special tokens of the DSL, and tokens for the results of earlier steps. At inference time it also applies masks from the grammar of the DSL at every decoding step, to keep the program well formed [@chen2021finqa]. Its output space is narrower than that of the syntax grammar of this chapter, which lets any number be written. A grammar that restricts the numbers to those of the page in the same way is not run in this book (@sec-other-things). ::: {.callout-tip title="Further reading"} - @dong2024xgrammar describe `xgrammar`, the library used here. - @tam2024speak study the effect of format restrictions on reasoning. ::: ## Summary - A grammar sets the probability of every token it does not allow to zero and leaves the rest as the model had them. At the start of a DSL answer, 39 of 151\,936 tokens remain. - On validation turns with predicted history, the grammar takes the untuned DSL from 57\.2% to 60\.4% and untuned Python from 64\.5% to 68\.4%, and invalid answers nearly disappear. The fine-tuned model is unchanged (83\.5% to 83\.6%). - The gain is under half of the invalid output removed, and mostly on program turns. The grammar closes 12\.5% of the gap between the untuned and the fine-tuned model; the ceiling is below the fine-tuned accuracy. - The grammar helps with the plain and the description prompt alike, and, with no examples, takes the model from the floor to 20\.8%. - The bounded number rule removes the runaway digits and does not change accuracy. - These are validation results. The final results do not repeat the grammar comparison on the development data.
